reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Olivier is getting a first haircut at a salon.
story:
Olivier sat in a big chair. It was his first haircut. The barber put a cape on him. It looked like a superhero cape.

The barber held a spray bottle. "Squirt, squirt," it went. Water fell on Olivier's hair. Olivier laughed. Now his hair was wet. The wet hair lay flat and smooth. "I can fix your hair now," said the barber. "Wet hair is easy to cut."

Snip, snip, snip. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the cape. They looked like tiny pieces of the sky falling. Olivier patted them. "The hairs fell because you cut them," he said. "Yes, clever boy," said the barber. "One snip, and down they come."

After the haircut, they got a treat. Olivier had a yummy cookie. He looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I look like Daddy," he said. The barber laughed. "Same snips," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Jacob is getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office.
story:
Jacob sat in the car with his mama. The seat was warm from the sun. The steering wheel was too hot to touch, so Mama used a cloth to turn it.

"We will see Nurse Bev today," said Mama. "You will get a little shot." Jacob held his toy bunny tight. He did not like shots. Shots gave a quick pinch.

At the doctor's office, Jacob saw a picture of a yellow flower on the wall. Nurse Bev came in with a small tray. "Time for your turn," she said kindly. Jacob squeezed his bunny. Then Nurse Bev said, "Take a big breath. Now cough, like this." Jacob took a big breath. He coughed, a big loud cough. The shot went in and out so fast. It hid inside the cough, like a bunny hiding in the grass.

"All done," said Nurse Bev. She put a round bandage on his leg. On the bandage was a tiny white flower. Jacob looked at it and coughed again, just for fun. "One more big cough," he said. Nurse Bev laughed and clapped her hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Jaxson sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green.
story:
Jaxson wanted to paint a cat at daycare. But he could not find the color orange. He looked in the paint cup. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. He saw blue paint. He saw green paint. No orange at all.

He asked his teacher, Miss Maya. "Where is the orange paint?"

Miss Maya smiled. "Try mixing two colors. Watch what happens."

Jaxson dipped his brush in red. He put red on the paper. Then he dipped in yellow. He put yellow on top of the red. He stirred it with his brush. The spot turned orange!

"Wow," said Jaxson. "Red and yellow make orange!"

He wanted to see more. He tried blue and yellow. The paint turned green, like grass. He tried red and blue. It made purple, like a plum. What a fun day for colors!

Then he spilled a little blue paint. It ran into the yellow. Green spread across the table. "Look," said Jaxson. "The spill made green too!"

His friend Mia came over. "Paint my cat striped," she said.

Jaxson painted her cat. One stripe orange. One stripe green. One stripe purple. "One, two, three stripes," he counted.

Miss Maya held up the paper to dry. "What will red and green make?" she asked.

Jaxson dipped his brush to find out.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Ivy sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
story:
Ivy did not want to sleep. She wanted to slide at the park. "Can we go to the park now?" she asked. "No," said Mom. "It is bedtime now. The park is closed now. We can go tomorrow."

Tomorrow. Ivy wondered about that word. Today they had played in the sand. Yesterday they had eaten pancakes. Was tomorrow a real day? Would it ever come?

The clock ticked. "Now we brush teeth," said Mom. "Later we read a book." First teeth, then a book. Things came one by one, like steps.

Ivy woke up in the morning. Sun was on her bed. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. "It is today," said Mom with a smile. "Yesterday's tomorrow is today!"

Ivy felt dizzy from so much thinking. Then she laughed. She reached for her shoes. The day came after the night. Sleep made tomorrow come. "Park now!" she said, and Mom opened the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Jake sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later.
story:
Yesterday, Jake went to the store with Mom. He saw a big red apple. He wanted it, but Mom said, "Not today. We have apples at home."

Today, Jake went to the store again. He held Mom's hand. He looked for the red apples. But the apple bin was empty!

"Where did they go?" Jake asked.

A store man pointed to a box. New apples were still in the box. "The apples go on the shelf later," he said. "First, we wash them now."

Jake watched the store man. The man turned on the water. He rinsed each apple. The apples got shiny and wet. Then he set them in a big bin, one by one.

"Can I help?" Jake asked.

"Yes," said the man. "You can put this apple right here."

Jake put the apple in the bin. It rolled a little. Then it sat still, next to the others.

"One more," said the man. Jake set it down soft. This time it did not roll.

"You love apples too?" the man asked.

"Yes," said Jake. "I love them in my kitchen."

Mom smiled. "Now we can buy one," she said. "And tomorrow, we can eat apple slices at home."

Jake picked the shiniest apple. "This one," he said. "It is the first one I helped with."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Hunter is learning something new. What Hunter is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
story:
Hunter stood by the counter in the kitchen. Mom had made warm toast for him. Now he wanted to put the butter on all by himself.

He held the soft butter knife. He pressed too hard. The toast broke into two pieces. "Oh no," said Hunter. Mom smiled and gave him a new slice. "Press gently this time," she said. Hunter tried again. He made slow, soft strokes. The butter went on in a smooth, yellow path. The whole toast was covered.

Next came the milk. Hunter picked up the big cup. He poured fast. Milk sloshed over the top. He stopped and took a breath. Then he tipped the carton slowly. The milk slid down the side and filled the cup to the middle. Not one drop spilled. Hunter took a bite of his buttery toast. He drank his milk in one big, happy gulp. "I did it, Mom! All by myself!"

activity: Through what Joshua sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
story:
Joshua wanted his toy lion. It was circle time at daycare. He could not find it.

The toy box was a big mess. Cars sat with the plastic apple. The duck sat with the blocks. Miss Amy came to help. "Let us sort them," she said. Joshua picked up a banana. It was plastic, so it went in the food bin. He picked up a cow. The cow was a toy animal, so it went in the animal bin.

He did try to find the lion in every bin. The lion was not near the top. It was under a soft rabbit. Joshua pulled it out. "There you are!" he said. The lion got a big hug.

Then his friend Ben looked sad. Ben could not find his doctor kit. Joshua looked in the toy bin. There was the little medicine bottle, right next to the blocks. He gave it to Ben.

"Now the bins are neat," said Miss Amy. Joshua clapped his hands and made the lion roar.

activity: Through what Nathan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the days of the week, the months and the idea that a calendar shows when things happen.
story: Nathan did not want to sleep. He had a question in his head. "When does Grandma come?" he asked. Daddy said, "Let's look at the calendar." Daddy lifted Nathan up so he could see. The calendar had rows of little squares. Grandma's picture was in one square. "See her smiley face?" said Daddy. "She comes on that day." Nathan touched the square. He could not make it be tomorrow. That made his tummy hurt a little. Daddy pointed to the top. "These are the days. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday," he said. Then he turned the page. A new month fell down, flat like a flag. "The month changed today," Daddy said. Nathan felt the paper. It was cold, like his frozen toes on the floor. Daddy tucked him in. Every morning, Nathan crossed off one square with his crayon. The smiley face came closer and closer. At last the square with Grandma was next. Nathan crossed off the last little square and ran to the door in his pajamas. Grandma was already knocking. "You found me!" she laughed, and Nathan held up the calendar for her to see.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Jasper sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the days of the week, the months and the idea that a calendar shows when things happen.
story:
Jasper wanted to ride his bike at school. "Bike Day comes on Friday," said Miss Kim. Jasper could not wait.

Miss Kim pointed at the wall. There was a big paper calendar. It had rows and rows of squares. Each square had a name. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. "See this square?" said Miss Kim. "This one is Friday."

Every morning, Jasper ran to the calendar. Monday, he moved the red magnet one square. Tuesday, he moved it again. On Thursday, he used a sharp pencil to draw a little bike on the Friday square. "That is my bike," he told his friend Milo. Milo laughed. "It looks like a duck!" said Milo. Jasper laughed too.

On Friday morning, Jasper wore his helmet to school. He looked at the calendar. The red magnet sat on the bike square. Outside, the bikes were lined up by the fence. Jasper ran to his bike and rang the bell. Ding, ding!

activity: Charles is learning something new. What Charles is learning: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet.
story:
Charles ran to the table. His sandwich was waiting. He grabbed it with sticky hands.

"Hold on," said Mom. "Your hands have jam on them." She turned on the tap. The water was warm, not hot. Mom held his hands under it. Then she put soap on his palms.

"Make bubbles," she said. Charles rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles turned pink. "Where did the jam go?" he asked. "Into the bubbles!" said Mom. Charles giggled. The jam was hiding in the foam.

They counted together. One, two, three, all the way to twenty. Then the bubbles swirled down the drain. Gone! His hands were clean and shiny.

Charles picked up his sandwich. He took a big bite. His milk was cold and sweet. After lunch, he ran to the potty by himself. Then he hurried back to the sink. More bubbles, pink or white, swirling away. "Bye bye, germs," he whispered. "See you never!"

activity: Through what Charlotte sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
story:
Charlotte went to the park with her toy picnic basket. Inside were a plastic apple, a wooden cookie, and two real peas in a paper cup. She wanted to give a picnic to the ducks.

A big white duck came near. Charlotte held out the wooden cookie. The duck looked at it. The duck did not eat it. Then Charlotte tipped the paper cup. The two real peas fell on the grass. The duck gobbled them up fast. "The duck eats real food," said Charlotte. "It does not eat toys."

Next to the pond, Charlotte began to build a little tower of pebbles. It was a magic castle for the ducks. A small brown animal hopped by. It had wet fur and a funny, ugly tail. It was a muskrat! It sniffed the tower, then slid into the water with a plop.

Charlotte laughed and waved. "More peas tomorrow!" she called. The duck flapped its wings and quacked back.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Rowan is welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family.
story:
Rowan went to the hospital with Dad. Mom was in a big bed. Next to her was a small basket. In the basket was a baby. "This is your sister," said Mom. "Her name is Ivy." Rowan stood very still. Ivy was tiny. She had little hands and little feet.

Then Ivy began to cry. Her face turned red. Her cries were loud like a storm. Rowan wanted her to stop. He did not know what to do. Mom said, "Try holding her hand." Rowan put out one finger. Ivy grabbed it. She held on tight. But she still cried.

"Maybe she needs a soft song," said Mom. Rowan sang a little song. He sang it once. Ivy kept crying. He sang it again, slow and quiet. Ivy's eyes looked up. Her crying got small. Then it stopped. "Again," whispered Dad. Rowan sang one more time. "You helped her," said Mom. Rowan smiled and counted Ivy's small toes. One, two, three, four, five. Ivy held his finger the whole time.

activity: Through what Luke sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the idea that plants and animals need food, water and a place to live.
story:
Luke's tomato plant looked sad. Its leaves hung down low. Luke touched the dirt. The dirt was dry and cracked.

Luke wanted his plant to grow big. He climbed onto a stool by the sink. He filled a small cup with water. Then he climbed back down. He poured the water on the dirt. It made a soft, happy sound.

The next morning, Luke ran to the window. The leaves stood up tall. "It was thirsty," Luke said. "Water helped it."

Then Luke heard a tiny scratch at the door. A small brown cat sat on the step. It drank from a puddle. Then it curled up in the warm box Luke kept on the porch. Luke put a little food in a bowl too. The cat ate it all. Then it rubbed its back on Luke's leg and purred.

"You need water, food and a home," Luke said. "Just like my plant." The cat blinked at him and went to sleep in the box.

activity: Through what Kayden sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
story:
Kayden went to the store with Mama. He wanted a soft toy bear. He wanted a red crayon too. Kayden counted his wishes. One, the bear. Two, the crayon. Three, a cookie.

The bear was up too high on the shelf. Kayden could not reach it. He pulled a chair. It tipped over. Blocks fell and began to sweep across the floor. Kayden looked around. He said, "Sorry, I knocked the blocks down." A store lady smiled. "Thank you for telling me," she said.

Kayden asked, "Can you help me, please?" The lady reached up high. She put the soft bear in his hands. Kayden hugged it. "Thank you!" he said. He saw the red crayon down low. He got it all by himself. At the counter, Mama paid. Kayden got the cookie too. Three wishes, three happy things. The lady waved. "Please come back soon," she said. Kayden waved his bear's paw.

activity: Through what Audrey sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
story:
Audrey sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house. But her tummy felt funny. "Are we almost there?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Daddy. "It is far away."

Audrey wanted her bunny. Bunny was a toy. But bunny was home in her bed. Audrey felt sad. Then she looked out the window. A cow stood in the grass. A dog ran by a fence. "Animals!" said Audrey. She counted them. "One cow. One dog."

Then she saw a big truck. It was full of apples. "Food," said Audrey. "I see food!" Her tummy growled.

Daddy heard it. He was gentle and slow. He reached into his bag. He found a banana. "Food for you," he said.

Audrey ate the banana. It was soft and sweet. The cow went away because the car drove past. Audrey waved bye-bye.

Soon her eyes felt heavy. "Can I have a nap?" she asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. "I will wake you at Grandma's."

Audrey closed her eyes. The car went hum, hum, hum. She held the banana peel in her hand. Daddy held her hand when she woke up, and Grandma's door was right there.

activity: Lillian is getting a first haircut at a salon.
story:
Lillian sat in a big chair. It went up, up, up. She looked around the salon. There were mirrors everywhere.

"I see two of me!" said Lillian. "Why are there two?" She waved one hand. Both girls in the mirror waved too. "Oh," she said. "The mirror makes a copy of me."

The hairdresser, Rosa, put a cape on Lillian. It was blue with white circles. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down. One bit landed on the cape. It sat in a circle shape. Lillian watched it.

"My hair is missing from my head now," said Lillian. "Where did it go?" She pointed at the floor. "It fell down because you cut it," she said. Rosa smiled and nodded.

Rosa turned the chair slowly. The mirror showed the back of Lillian's head. "That is me too," said Lillian. She patted her short hair and grinned at the girl in the glass.

activity: Nathan is losing a first wobbly tooth.
story:
Nathan sat at the dinner table. He had corn on his plate. He had a big smile too. "My tooth is wobbly!" he said. Mom leaned in close. "Let me see," she said. Nathan opened his mouth wide. The tooth wiggled from side to side. "Wow," said Dad. "That tooth is getting loose. That is a sign a new tooth is coming."

Nathan wanted that tooth out. He bit the corn. Click. The tooth wiggled more. He bit again. Click, click. It wiggled even more. "Eat your apple slice," said Mom. Nathan bit the apple. Then he felt something small and hard. He put his finger in his mouth. The tooth was in his hand!

"Look! Look!" Nathan shouted. Dad laughed. Mom clapped her hands. Nathan ran to the mirror. There was a little gap in his smile. He smiled bigger. Then he ran back to the table and held up his tooth. "Apple wins!" he said.

activity: Through what Jaxson sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green.
story:
Jaxson sat at the paint table. His cup held blue paint. His friend Mia had yellow paint.

"Can we mix them?" asked Jaxson.

"Try it," said Mia.

Jaxson dipped his brush in blue. He dipped it in yellow too. Then his elbow bumped the table. Uh oh. The blue cup tipped over. The blue paint would spill!

Splat. Blue paint ran into the yellow tray.

Jaxson looked very hard. Where did the blue go? Where did the yellow go? Now there was something new. It was green! He touched it with one finger.

"One dot, two dots, three dots," he said. "Green dots."

He looked at Mia. "The blue went into the yellow. Now it is green!"

Mia poured more yellow. Jaxson poured more blue. They mixed it with the brush. Round and round it went. Green again!

"One pot, two pots, three pots of green!" said Mia.

Teacher Kim came over. "What a big green lake," she said.

"We made it," said Jaxson. "Blue and yellow made green."

Then Mia held up her striped sock. "Look! Blue stripes and yellow stripes. Still blue and yellow."

Jaxson laughed. "Paint is different. Paint makes green!"

He painted one green frog, one green leaf, one green ball.

activity: Penelope is learning something new. What Penelope is learning: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name.
story:
Penelope sat at the little table. Her teacher gave her a pencil. "Now we write our names," said the teacher.

Penelope squeezed the pencil in her whole fist. She pushed hard. The letter P came out fat and wobbly. The pencil point snapped off and flew across the table. "Oh no," said Penelope. "Why did it break?" She looked at the pencil.

Her friend Ben sat next to her. He held his pencil with just three fingers, light as a coin resting on his hand. His letters came out small and neat. Penelope tried again. She held the pencil with three fingers too. She did not push hard. The P came out round and clear. Then the E. Then the N. She wrote every letter all the way to the last one.

"Look, I did it!" said Penelope. The teacher smiled and taped the paper up on the wall. Penelope stood and looked at her name, big and proud, above the coat hooks.

activity: Luna is learning something new. What Luna is learning: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal.
story:
Luna walked with her father to the festival. The tables were long and bright. There were many people, and big bowls of food.

Everyone sat down, but nobody ate. Luna looked around. "Why is no one eating?" she asked. Her grandmother smiled. "Watch," she said. Grandma put her hands together. Then all the people put their hands together too. Grandma said the greeting, loud and clear. "We thank the food and the hands that made it." Everyone said it with her.

Luna put her little hands together. She said the words too. Some were new words. She said them softly, then louder. When the last word was done, everyone picked up bread at the same time. First the words, then the bread. It was like a magic key.

Luna felt proud. She turned to the small boy next to her. He looked sad and had no bread yet. Luna picked up a big warm piece. She put it on his plate. "Now we say it together next time," she said. The boy smiled big. Luna put her hands together again, just for fun. "Thank you, bread," she whispered, and took a big bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Joshua sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods.
story:
Joshua liked the sorting game at daycare. Teacher May put out three baskets. One basket was for animals. One was for toys. One was for foods.

Joshua found a little plastic cow. He put the cow in the animal basket. Then he found a ball. The ball went in the toy basket. Then he found a banana. It looked like his toy duck, yellow and small. He put the banana in the animal basket.

Teacher May held up the banana. "The banana is a food," she said. "We can eat it." Joshua tried to think. "The cow is not a food," he said. "The cow is an animal." He put the banana in the food basket, near the apple and the bread.

Next, Joshua found a small bottle. It was from the doctor kit. It was pretend medicine. "Medicine is not a food," Joshua said. He put it with the doctor toys. The basket for toys was full now.

Joshua clapped his hands. "Sorting is fun," he said. Teacher May gave him a big smile. "You are a good sorter, Joshua." Joshua picked up the toy cow and made it say, "Moo!"

activity: Through what Ethan sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules.
story:
Ethan ran to Grandpa's house. His cousin Mia was there too. Grandpa held a jar with one coin inside. "You can both play my game," Grandpa said. "One turn each. That is the rule."

Mia went first. She dropped the coin in the slot and it rang. Ding! Now Ethan wanted the coin. He grabbed it fast. Mia's lip shook and her eyes got wet.

Grandpa knelt down. "Ethan, she has not had a turn yet."

Ethan looked at Mia. He held out the coin. "Your turn," he said.

Mia smiled. Ding! Then she handed it back. "Your turn," she said.

Ethan dropped the coin. Ding! The furry dog came to lick his hand. "Turns make it fair," Ethan said. Ding! Ding! They played all afternoon.

activity: Through what Isabella sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting.
story:
Isabella went to the library with her family. She saw a shelf of shiny books. Ten little books sat in a row. "I will count them," she said. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, um, um." Oh no. The next number ran away from her mouth.

Then she heard singing in the story room. A girl sang, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Isabella bent down to peek through the door. The song had all the numbers! The numbers liked to march in a line, just like the books. She whispered the song twice. The numbers came back to her.

"Can I count your books too?" she asked the singing girl. "Yes! Count with me." Isabella pointed at each book. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She did not get stuck at all. The singing girl clapped. Isabella held up ten fingers and sang the numbers one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Arthur is searching for a lost favorite toy.
story:
Arthur lost his favorite dinosaur at daycare. He looked in the block corner. He looked under the art table. "One, two, three," he counted the places he had checked.

Then Arthur saw something funny. His friend Mia had green paint on her hands. She made green dots on the floor. Dot, dot, dot. The dots went past the sink. Arthur looked down at his own hands. He had green paint too! The dinosaur had been in his pocket, and paint from his hands had rubbed off. Maybe he had made a trail.

Arthur followed the dots. Dot, dot, dot. They went to the dress-up box. Mia came to help. "You share your dinosaur," she said. "I will share my looking." They peeked in the box. There was a green smudge on a hat. Under the hat sat the dinosaur!

"One, two, three, hooray!" said Arthur. He hugged the dinosaur tight. Then he washed the paint off his hands with Mia, so the next trail would only be clean.

activity: Harper is getting through an evening power cut at home.
story:
Harper was playing in the backyard. The sky got dark. Then all the lights in the house went out. The porch light went out too. Harper stood very still.

Mom came outside with a candle. "The power is out," she said. "It will come back soon." Harper looked at the dark house. She wanted her nightlight. She wanted her lamp with the bunny on it. Mom said the lamps needed power from the wires. No power meant no light.

Harper had an idea. She ran to her toy box near the fence. She dug and dug. She found her flashlight. She pushed the little button. The flashlight did not turn on. She turned it over and shook it. Mom smiled and waited. Harper tried again. Then she saw why. The batteries were old. Dad brought two new batteries from the kitchen drawer. Harper put them in, one by one, carefully. She pushed the button again. The light came on! A big bright circle shone on the grass.

"I did it," Harper said. She shone the light on the fence. She shone it on her tooth, which was wiggly, in the mirror by the door. Mom said, "Would you like to help bake biscuits tomorrow, when the oven has power again?" Harper nodded. They sat on the step together. Harper held the flashlight steady. The sky got darker. The stars came out, one, then two, then many. Then the porch light clicked back on, all by itself. Harper clapped her hands and said, "The power came home!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Noah is starting the first day of school.
story:
Noah stood at the classroom door. He held his small blue bag. His mama gave him a hug. Then she waved and walked away.

Noah looked around. He saw toys. He saw paint. He saw other kids. He did not know where to put his bag. He set it on the floor. Then he went to play with a truck.

A boy ran by. He tripped on the bag. The trucks fell over. Noah looked at the bag on the floor. "The bag was in the way," Noah said. He felt a little lost.

The teacher knelt down. She pointed to little boxes on the wall. Each box had a name on it. Noah saw his own name. It was a green square. Noah put his bag in his square. The floor was clear now. No one would trip.

The boy with the trucks smiled at Noah. "You can play too," he said. Noah sat down. He pushed a red truck across the rug. It zoomed right to the wall.

"Your name shows your spot," Noah said. The teacher nodded. Noah made the truck zoom again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Elias sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
story:
Elias wanted to find the ice cream truck at the park. He could not hear it. He cupped his hands behind his ears. "Listen, ears," he said. Then he heard it. Ring, ring, ring!

The truck stopped by the wooden bench. Elias smelled something sweet. His nose knew that smell. He ran to Mama. "Ice cream!" he said.

Mama bought a small cone. Elias licked it with his tongue. Cold and sweet. Then the sun made the ice cream soft. A drop began to fall. "It will fall!" said Elias. Mama held out her hand. The drop fell on her fingers, not his shoe.

Elias touched the bench with his fingers. The wood felt warm and bumpy. "My eyes saw the truck," he said. "My ears heard it. My nose smelled it. My tongue tasted it. My fingers touched it." He looked at his cone. All gone. He giggled and said, "Again tomorrow?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Hailey is attending a religious or cultural celebration with family.
story:
Hailey ran to the table. It was Hanukkah, her favorite night. She saw the menorah with its shiny candles.

"Can I put one in?" she asked Grandma. Grandma smiled and gave her a candle. Hailey pushed it into the holder. It stood up tall. Then Grandma lit the candles. Hailey watched the little flames. One flame leaned over. A drop of hot wax fell on Hailey's arm. It felt itchy. She rubbed it soft with her sleeve. "The flame moved because the window is open," said Grandma. She closed the window. The flames stood very still.

Then Hailey looked close. There was a big, soft pillow on her chair. Under the pillow was one more candle. A secret candle! "You found the helper candle," said Grandma. "It lights all the rest." Hailey held it gently. "So the flames come from this one," she said. Grandma nodded. "Now I learn something new every night," said Hailey. She snuggled into the pillow and watched the candles glow. "Can we do nine candles tomorrow?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Nolan is learning something new. What Nolan is learning: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done.
story:
Nolan was at Mia's house. He wanted to draw a big cat. But first he had to find the cat.

"Where is the draw place?" Nolan asked.

"You mean the tablet," Mia said. She pulled it out from under the couch. "Press the round button on top. Hold it until the screen wakes up."

Nolan pressed it once. Nothing happened. He pressed it fast, three times. Nothing.

"You have to hold it," said Mia. "Like holding a door handle. You wait."

Nolan held the button down. He counted, "One, two, three." The screen lit up like morning.

"Oh! It likes a long press," Nolan said. "It does not like a fast press."

He slid his finger across the smooth screen. He found the blue square with a crayon on it. He tapped it. The drawing app opened. Nolan drew a cat with orange stripes. He gave the cat four socks, one on each paw. "Silly cat," he said. "Cats do not wear socks."

When he was done, Mia showed him the round home button. Nolan pressed it and held it. "Slide this bar," Mia said. The screen went dark.

Nolan put the tablet back under the couch, right where it lived. "Bye, cat," he whispered. "Sleep well."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Samuel is learning something new. What Samuel is learning: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves.
story:
Samuel wanted to play outside. The snow was falling. His coat hung on the hook by the door.

He pulled the coat off the hook. He pushed his arms in. One arm went in fine. The other arm bumped the side and would not go in. The coat was on backwards. The hood sat on his nose.

"Try it the other way," said Mama.

Samuel took the coat off. He turned it around. Both arms went in this time. The hood sat on his head, right where it should.

Now came the zipper. Samuel found the little rough tab. He pushed it down into the slider. It made a small click. The two sides of the coat came together. He pulled the tab up, up, up. The zipper closed all the way to his chin.

Samuel looked down at himself. The zipper made a long line from his belly to his chin. The coat was warm and snug.

"I did it," he said.

"Zipper up, coat on," said Mama. "Ready for snow."

Samuel opened the door. The cold air touched his cheeks. He ran out and made the first snowball of the day.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Levi is spending a surprise snow day at home.
story:
Levi woke up and saw white everywhere. Snow! School was closed. It was a snow day at home. Mom said they could walk next door to visit Mrs. Bell. Levi put on his big red boots. Every step made a deep mark in the snow. He looked back and laughed. His boots made footprints, one for each foot!

But Mrs. Bell's front steps were covered in ice. Levi slipped and sat down in the snow. "Watch out," said Mrs. Bell. She took out a big box of salt. She shook the salt all over the steps. Would that help? Levi sat in the snow and watched.

Soon the ice began to melt. It got shiny and wet. Then it was gone! Levi walked up the steps. His boots did not slip at all. Inside, Mrs. Bell gave him a juicy orange slice. It dripped down his chin. "More salt," said Levi, "makes more melting!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Luna is learning something new. What Luna is learning: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal.
story:
Luna walked with her father to the festival. There were bright flags and a big table full of food. Everyone sat down, but nobody ate yet.

Luna was hungry. "Why are we waiting?" she asked. Her father put his hands together, palms flat. He held them near his chest. Luna looked around. All the grown-ups did the same thing with their hands.

So Luna put her hands together too. First she put them under her chin. That felt wobbly, and her hands slipped. Then she put them near her chest, like her father. They stayed still. She said the new words after him, one at a time. "Thank you for our food."

After the words, everyone picked up a plate. Luna picked up a little bread. "We eat now," she said, "because the hands came together first." Her grandmother smiled and put a sweet plum on her bread.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Lydia sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations.
story:
Lydia got to daycare early. Only one friend was there. It was Ben, and he looked sad.

"I miss my mama," Ben said.

Lydia wanted to help. She looked around. She saw the little kitchen corner. It had a red pot and small cups. She picked up a cup. She tipped it over Ben's doll. "Drink your milk," she said in a big voice.

Ben stopped crying. He picked up the doll. He patted its back, very soft. "There, there," he said.

Then Lydia got a blanket. She wrapped the doll up. Ben held it close. The doll got a hug.

"Let's play house," Lydia said. "You be the dad." Ben nodded. He made soup in the red pot. He stirred it with a big spoon. It smelled like nothing, but he sniffed it anyway. "Mmm," he said.

Lydia rocked the doll. It went to sleep, just like that. Ben smiled now.

The teacher came over. "Is the baby warm?" she asked.

"Yes," said Ben. He tucked the blanket under the doll's chin.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Jasper is cooking or baking a meal for the family.
story:
Jasper woke up in the big green tent. The birds were singing outside. He sat up and looked for his shoes.

"Daddy, can we make breakfast?" he asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. "Let's cook eggs at the campsite."

Jasper helped carry the little blue bowl. He carried the spoon, too. Daddy lit the camp stove. Jasper stayed back, just like Daddy said. Daddy cracked the eggs into the pan.

Jasper watched the eggs. They were wobbly and wet. Then they sat in the hot pan. Slowly, the wobbly eggs turned flat and white.

"Look, Daddy! The eggs changed!" said Jasper.

"The hot pan cooks them," said Daddy.

Jasper found a stick on the ground. He poked at the dirt with it. His toy elephant sat nearby on the log. Jasper gave the elephant a pretend egg on a leaf plate.

Mommy came out of the tent, yawning. Baby sister was still asleep on Mommy's back.

"Breakfast is ready," said Daddy.

They all sat on the log together. Jasper ate his eggs from a red plate. The eggs were warm and soft. Mommy ate her eggs, too.

"Mmm," said Mommy. "These are good eggs."

Jasper looked at his elephant. He patted its gray head.

"You can have more later," Jasper told the elephant.

Daddy poured warm milk into Jasper's cup. Jasper drank it all up. Then he put his elephant on his lap and shared the last bite of egg, just pretend, on the empty spoon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Mohamed is learning something new. What Mohamed is learning: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling.
story:
Mohamed ran into the kitchen. "I want to make my own breakfast!" he said.

Mama smiled. "The toast is ready. Here is the butter." She put a dull, round knife in his hand. "Not a sharp one," she said. "This one is safe for you."

Mohamed dipped the knife into the butter. He pressed hard on the toast. The toast tore! A little hole stared up at him.

"Too hard," said Mama. "Try soft and slow."

Mohamed tried again. He touched the knife lightly. The butter slid like a soft blanket. The whole toast turned golden. "Look!" he shouted.

"Now the milk," said Mama. She gave him a small jug.

Mohamed lifted it high. Milk splashed onto the table. He looked at the puddle.

Mama put a cloth down. "Keep the jug close to the cup," she said. "Not high up."

Mohamed filled the cup again. This time the jug stayed low. The milk went glug, glug. Not one drop fell. The cup sat full and white.

"Breakfast time!" he called.

Mohamed bit into his toast. It was buttery all the way to the edges. He drank his milk. "I did it all by myself," he said. "Tomorrow I want to pour juice too!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Everly sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations.
story:
Everly sat on the big red slide. Her teddy bear sat in her lap. But teddy looked sad. His hat was gone. "Where is your hat?" she asked. Teddy did not answer. Only the wind answered. It went whoosh in the trees.

Then Everly saw something small and yellow. It was under the bench. It was teddy's hat! The wind had blown it there. She ran over and picked it up. "Found it!" she said.

Her mom sat close by on the bench. "Can we play house?" Everly asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, we can." So teddy wore his hat. Everly gave him a quick hug. She held a leaf to his mouth like a little cup. "Drink your milk," she said. Teddy sat warm in the sun. Everly rocked him in her arms. "Night night, teddy," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Through what Willow sees, hears and does, the story naturally introduces polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help.
story:
Willow wanted jam on her toast. She pulled her stool to the counter and began to climb up. "Can you help me, please?" she asked. "I can hold the jam jar."

"Of course," said Dad. He spread the jam with a safe knife. The jar was heavy, so he held it low for her.

Willow reached out. The jar tipped over. Red jam splatted on the floor. "Oh no," said Willow. "I am sorry, Dad."

"That is okay," said Dad. "Will you help me wipe it up?"

"Yes, please give me a cloth," said Willow. She wiped the jam in little circles. Sticky spots stayed on the tiles. She wiped them again. Then the floor looked tidy and clean again.

Dad put a fresh slice of bread in the toaster. Soon the toast popped up, warm and brown. Willow sniffed the yummy smell. Dad spread soft butter and red jam.

"Thank you, Dad!" said Willow. She took a big bite. The jam was sweet on her tongue. Dad sat beside her with his own toast.

Willow smiled at him. "Your toast too?" she asked. "Yes, please," said Dad, "and one more jam jar for us to share."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Olivier is getting a first haircut at a salon.
story:
Olivier sat in a big chair. The chair was very tall. His papa stood next to him.

The barber put a cape on Olivier. The cape was blue like the sky. It went swish, swish. Olivier laughed.

"I want to fix your hair," said the barber. "Snip, snip!" The scissors went snip. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. Snip, snip. More pieces fell. They fell like tiny rain.

Olivier looked down. The hair made a little pile. He patted the pile with his hand. The hair was soft. Some hair stuck to his hand! He shook his hand. The hair flew off. "Bye bye, hair," he said.

The barber brushed Olivier's head. The brush tickled. "Ha ha!" said Olivier.

Then Papa picked him up. The barber gave Olivier a red lollipop. "Is it yummy?" asked the barber. Olivier took a big lick. "Yummy," he said.

The cape came off with one more swish. All the little hairs stayed on the floor. Olivier waved at them. "Bye bye!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: Miles is starting the first day of school.
story:
Miles stood at the school gate. He held his dad's hand very tight. The gate was big and red. Miles did not want to go in.

A teacher opened the gate. "Hello! I am Miss Ana," she said. "Everyone wears a name tag today. Then new friends can meet you." She put a tag on Miles. It said his name in blue letters.

A girl looked at his tag. "Your name is Miles!" she said. "I am Tia. Want to draw?" Miles sat down at the little table. Tia gave him a red crayon. He drew a big sun. "My mom drew a sun on my tag," said Tia. "She is my special helper."

Miles smiled. "Dad is my helper too," he said. "He waits at the gate." Then he drew a small red gate next to his sun.
